rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mount Ṭūr and the Torah witness to the divine law of retribution: the Torah records past nations' punishments, showing the law has endured since Adam and will culminate in complete justice, punishment for evil, and recompense for good.
rows.anchor: mount Ṭūr is a historical sign of the divine law of retribution

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form of kitāb heightens its grandeur: the Torah was the first revealed scripture to record prophetic teachings in writing, whereas earlier prophetic guidance was mostly oral.
rows.anchor: is not defined by a definite article is meant to heighten its grandeur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book's open pages make its conclusive communication public: nothing is concealed, anyone can read it, and those unable to read may hear it or ask its bearers to read it aloud.
rows.anchor: nothing is concealed in it; everything is openly available in its spread out sheets and anyone can read it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs acknowledged the People of the Book's religious learning and claimed Abraham and Ishmael as forefathers, the Torah lets them check whether their ancestors warned of the Day of reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān at many instances has directed them to ask from the People of the Book what they do not know.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the pages spread out subtly censures Jews for concealing scripture; the Qur’an elsewhere notes this concealment, which Islahi says arose in their period of decline.
rows.anchor: also carries a subtle aspersion on the Jews of the times of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews hid Torah predictions of the final Prophet, fearing that people would learn of the threatened divine wrath and loss of their leadership if they rejected him; Jesus' lamp-under-a-cup rebuke illustrates their concealment.
rows.anchor: In these predictions, they were threatened that if they denied this prophet, they would invite God’s wrath and be deprived of their position of leadership

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes commonly identify the populated house as a heavenly house for angels, analogous to the Baytullah for people; Islahi rejects this because it does not evidence the oath's claim, which depends on evidentiary force rather than sacredness.
rows.anchor: Generally our exegetes have interpreted this expression to

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some identify the populated house as the Baytullah; Islahi considers this more tenable than the heavenly-house interpretation because the Kaaba lies in the secure city invoked to substantiate reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: Some people regard this expression to refer to the Baytull āh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the Kaaba reading in context: the following lofty roof is the heavens, not the Kaaba's roof, and the sequence of Kaaba, heavens, and sea lacks the harmony linking Ṭūr with the written book.
rows.anchor: after this, the lofty roof is sworn by. Obviously, this cannot refer to the roof of the Baytull āh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies the populated house as the earth, with the sky as its roof; he calls it an apt metaphor and notes that the Qur’an also describes earth as a prepared resting place.
rows.anchor: refers to this earth extending over which is the roof of the sky.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His second reason for reading the populated house as earth is that the sky is mentioned immediately afterward, and the Qur’an commonly pairs earth and sky as signs of God.
rows.anchor: after its mention, a reference to the sky clearly shows that it refers to the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His third reason is that earth's provisions testify to human accountability; al-maʿmūr evokes both the resources people enjoy and their consequent liability to answer for benefiting from them.
rows.anchor: the various sources and resources the Almighty has made available in this earth bear witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His fourth reason links the oath to al-Dhāriyāt: signs on earth and in people, and heavenly sustenance alongside what is threatened, support retribution; the same evidence is used here in a different style.
rows.anchor: in the earth and yourselves also are signs for those who have conviction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He concludes that the populated house is earth, whose signs of God's power, wisdom, and providence substantiate divine justice and reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: refers to the earth and its qualification by the attribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the earth, the sky supplies the next witness; Islahi points to its role, along with winds and clouds, in the destruction of nations under divine wrath.
rows.anchor: how much role the sky, winds and clouds had in the destruction of nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the sky a roof evokes God's providence, graciousness, and mercy, like a vast tent stretched above humanity by grace.
rows.anchor: bears witness to the providence, graciousness and mercy of God:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the roof lofty evokes God's power, grandeur, and greatness; these divine attributes testify to the Hereafter and reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: alludes to God’s power, grandeur and greatness:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's providence and power witness to the Hereafter and to reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: attributes of God (providence and power)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi explains sajara as becoming brimful, illustrated by expressions for filling a stove with fuel and a canal with water.
rows.anchor: water became brimful in the canal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After earth and sky, the oceans are presented as a major earthly witness; Qur’anic passages likewise move from signs of heaven and earth to ocean signs of God's oneness, power, providence, and retribution.
rows.anchor: After presenting the witness of the heavens and the earth, in this verse the biggest sign on the earth ie. the oceans are presented as witness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened punishment has historical parallels in the oceanic calamities that struck Noah's people and Pharaoh; their accounts appear in both Torah and Qur’an.
rows.anchor: the threatened torment after the oaths can historically be seen in the account of Noah’s nation as well as in the fate of the Pharaoh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses state the certain, unavoidable punishment as the claim after the oaths and the sūra's central theme.
rows.anchor: These verses state the real claim after the oaths above

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim echoes al-Dhāriyāt 51:5–6, but al-Ṭūr gives greater prominence to punishment, making explicit what the preceding sūra had implied.
rows.anchor: The only difference is that in this sūrah the aspect of punishment is more prominent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi notes the Qur’anic pattern of first stating something concisely or implicitly and then elaborating it explicitly, as these sūras do.
rows.anchor: Elaborating upon what is stated in a concise manner first or explicitly mentioning something after its implicit mention is a very common style of the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing the Prophet, Islahi says the punishment mocked by Quraysh will certainly come and cannot be averted by their power, community, deities, or any rescuer in this world or the next.
rows.anchor: the punishment with which he is threatening the Quraysh and which they are making fun of is bound to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs already cited—the revelation to Moses at Ṭūr, Torah scriptures, earth, sky, and oceans—suffice to prove the claim; no further sign is needed.
rows.anchor: what is written in the scriptures of the Torah, the signs with which this earth is replete

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Quraysh see part of the sky fall, they may rejoice and mistake the torment for rain clouds, then persist in disbelief even as it destroys them.
rows.anchor: they will dance with glee thinking this torment to be rain-laden clouds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day the sky will reel and the mountains will be uprooted and move uncontrollably; this upheaval makes human power and fortifications useless.
rows.anchor: the sky which appears so stable, steady and strong in this world will start to reel and shake.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawr means moving here and there uneasily and restlessly, with parts of the sky moving in different directions.
rows.anchor: means “to move here and there uneasily and restlessly”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh mockingly asked what would happen to the mountains; Islahi says that when sky and mountains are overturned, human power, community, castles, and trenches will be no help, and elsewhere the Qur’an says God will crush the mountains.
rows.anchor: what use will anyone’s power or community, castles and trenches be for him!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woe on that Day means death and ruin for those denying the warning now.
rows.anchor: on that Day death and perdition will be for those who are denying it today.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description points to arrogant Quraysh who mocked, harassed the Prophet, and tried through babble to blunt his warnings; verses 29–46 elaborate on them.
rows.anchor: the arrogant people among the Quraysh who were trying to tease and harass the Prophet
